title: What the Victorians Knew About Making Leaders
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Aaron Renn uses a Works in Progress article on Victorian Britain's elites to critique modern meritocracy and the way America forms its leaders. The Victorian ruling class studied little by modern standards, worked short office days and socialized constantly, yet presided over the most successful country of its age. Their schools and universities emphasized classics, sport, student self-government and character formation rather than technical training, and the endless dinners and balls doubled as a dense network of trust and information. Renn argues that today's bureaucratic-professional model trains people to chase credentials and resume items, which breeds cynicism and leaves leaders unfit for unpopular decisions in the service of what is right. He adds Digby Baltzell's caution that formation is not enough, because an elite must also be open to talented outsiders to be seen as legitimate. The piece is a case for thinking about leadership as formation and community, not only competence and selection.
points: Victorian elites were formed through character-building schooling, sport and student self-government, which trained them to lead people rather than to master a technical domain.
Their heavy social life was functional work, building the trust, loyalty and information networks that held the ruling class together.
Renn contends that bureaucratic-professional selection, a term he prefers to meritocracy, produces cynical strivers and weakens institutional trust.
Formation alone is insufficient, since an elite must also admit qualified newcomers from all major groups to remain legitimate.
The managerial class that benefits from the current model is likely to resist leadership reform.
quotes: While never stating it directly, this piece stands as a major critique of the current idea of “meritocracy”-based elite selection and formation.
Despite this, the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful.

Technical-professional and managerial-bureaucratic skills have their necessary place in modern techno-industrial society, but when those values colonize institutional leadership, no surprise we see a dramatic decline in trust in those leaders and institutions.
Again, we see here preparation for being an actual leader, not just a master of a domain of technical or bureaucratic skills.

Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was neither training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.
Going through this process must instill in our young people a deeply cynical view of the world. It is certainly a process that inculcates values at odds with genuine leadership or statesmanship
While formation is important, we also can’t lose sight of the importance of selection.

Baltzell’s point, and it’s an important one, is that a nation’s upper class (which no longer truly exists in the US) and elite must include representatives of all the major groups in society to be considered legitimate.
